metadata.number_policy: HARD CONSTRAINT (series DOUBLE-CHECK LAW §B + author instruction 2026-09-01). NO performance figure appears anywhere in this episode — none is needed. The only performance number permitted anywhere in the season is ~0.85 AUROC (first-tier classifier), and it does not appear until E03. Approved non-performance figures HERE: ~2,400 years / 24 centuries; 80 million (2020); 111 million (2040); up to 40% nerve-fiber loss; 'more than a million' optic-nerve fibers. Banned: any second-tier accuracy or sensitivity; any AUROC in this episode.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Varun, and this video is about the silent thief of sight — why glaucoma is a pattern problem. Roughly twenty-four hundred years ago, in the age of Hippocrates, Greek physicians had a word for the pale, gray-green shimmer in a failing eye — glaukos. They had the name. They had no idea what caused it. Twenty-four centuries later, that disease is still a leading cause of blindness on Earth — and it's the reason this project exists.

props.command: Explain glaucoma to me the way a researcher would: what exactly does it destroy, why does nobody notice until it is too late, and why would anyone need an AI to catch it?
output: it destroys the optic nerve — from the edges inward
your own brain hides the damage until ~40% of fibers are gone
so detection is a pattern problem, not a looking problem

beats.series_slot: BLUF — added by EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW (not in the series doc; required by the chassis)
beats.narration_text: Glaucoma is a pattern problem. The damage is invisible to the eye that looks for it — so we're building a machine to read it instead. First, the enemy — and why it takes a machine.

props.text:
Glaucoma is a looking problem.
So we built a machine to read what the eye cannot.

shot.correction_rationale: SINGLE-TOKEN TRIGGER, by component constraint. BrutalistHesitantWriter.buildActs() splits the text on whitespace and matches triggers per token, so a multi-word trigger silently never corrects. Trigger is the lone token `looking` -> `pattern`. Read back with the replacement applied, the sentence stands alone as the episode's claim: 'Glaucoma is a pattern problem. The damage is invisible to the eye that looks for it - so we are building a machine to read it instead.' The word 'looks' in line 2 is a different token and is deliberately left untouched. Rendered via the reel-local UeOverviewWriter, registered at this beat's measured length (293f) so the correction is never trimmed off the tail.

beats.narration_text: The disease is glaucoma, and it is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. About eighty million people were living with it in 2020; by 2040, the projection is a hundred and eleven million. And two words make it a screening problem. Irreversible. And silent.

beats.narration_text: Here's what makes it merciless. Glaucoma attacks the optic nerve — a cable of more than a million fibers carrying every image from your eye to your brain. It kills them slowly, and it starts at the outside, working in. Not a blur. A subtraction.

beats.narration_text: And your brain covers for it. It fills the missing patches with what it expects to be there, so your vision feels whole. Feels fine. By the time you notice, you can have lost up to forty percent of those fibers — and they never grow back.

beats.narration_text: So we asked the question this whole series comes from. Could a machine read the damage an expert eye cannot perceive — and catch it early?

props.command: Draw me the difference between how a clinician reads an eye and how a model would: appearance judged by a human, versus a thickness measurement turned into numbers and scored for a pattern. Make it clear which signal survives the silent window.
output: two readings of the same eye — appearance vs measurement

beats.series_slot: BODY ¶4b — the concept taught (RESULT half of the ask→result pair)
beats.narration_text: The only way to win is to stop looking at the eye and start measuring it. Turn the nerve into numbers, then find the pattern that separates a dying nerve from a healthy one. That is not a looking problem. It's a pattern-recognition problem.

beats.narration_text: So that's the enemy: a disease that takes the nerve from the edges in, hides behind your own brain, and never gives anything back. Early detection isn't a nicety here. It's the only move.

beats.series_slot: YOUR TURN — series doc: 'If a disease gives no symptoms until it's too late — where would you even begin looking for it?'
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: pick a disease that stays silent until it's advanced. Tell me what measurable signal changes before any symptom appears, what it would cost to measure at population scale, and what the screening test would get wrong. That last clause is the one that matters — anything looks worth screening until you count the false alarms. Check that the answer names a signal, a cost, and a harm. If it skips the harm, push back.

props.command: Pick a disease that stays silent until it is advanced. Tell me what measurable signal changes BEFORE any symptom appears, what it would cost to measure at population scale, and what the screening test would get wrong. Then argue whether it is worth screening at all.

shot.scaffold_rubric: Spoken aloud, verbatim, then discussed: the answer must name (1) a signal, (2) a cost, (3) a harm. 'If it skips the harm, push back' gives the viewer the failure test — this is the scaffolded viewer task, not 'ask Claude about X'.
